I don't know. I find insurmountable problems with both options.

In the case of denser camera population the problems are easy to find. Privacy concerns obviously despite the claim of public spaces only. Logistically, 100% foolproof video is not acheivable. Even if the video is unaltered and of high quality, a perpetrator can easily disguise and deceive armed with the knowledge that everything is filmed. This is done even now. Think false flag events and even the benign feats of deception in a magician's show. You can't count on what you see and hear to 100% certainty. James Randi can tell you more about how easily people's senses can be manipulated.

For the fMRI the problems are with the technology. It would simply be so rigid that it could be manipulated itself. An interviewer only needs to ask their questions in certain orders and certain ways to illicit a desired response within the interviewed. This is already done with traditional polygraph. Similar tactics are employed when a child is guided to false truths about events like molestation. The detector, of any measure of technology, will only be as accurate as the user can or will allow for.

I'm still a proponent for the old arms race of intelligence and insight from trained detectives and lawyers to defend and convict people. It may be slow and cumbersome, but in the pursuit of condemning people I believe slow is best.

i prefer the fool proof fMRI lie detector, but i would only be comfortable with it in a government that had a strong sense of preserving liberty and only used it in cases where one person was abusing others. both scare the shit out of me because i expect bad actors to eventually come along and use these technologies for nefarious reasons. as such, i would expect all leaders to go through the foolproof fMRI to prove that they indeed were dedicated to the liberty and welfare of the people they were serving.
